text: Leveler is one of the most important additives for super-conformal copper electroplating, which has been widely applied in the fabrication of nanoscale (or microscale) interconnect features in integrated circuits (ICs) and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. In this study, a series of triphenylmethane-based (TPM-based) molecules with different nitrogen-containing groups have been designed, synthesized, and investigated as novel levelers for superconformal copper electroplating. Their structure-property relationships are investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It is found that the steric hindrance and the type of the nitrogen-containing groups (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) in a leveler not only affect its adsorption ratio and strength on the copper interface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different copper crystalline plane. In combination with Cl−, polyethylene glycol (PEG, suppressor), and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS, accelerator), all TPM-based levelers show excellent microvia filling performances in copper electroplating and their effective concentrations are related to their antagonistic ability against the accelerator SPS.

text: 1. Introduction
text_index: 1. Introduction
raw: 1. Introduction

text: Copper electrochemical deposition (ECD) for trench and microvia filling as interconnects in integrated circuits (ICs) or printed circuit boards (PCBs) is one of the most important techniques in modern electronic manufacturing industry [1,2]. For better stability and reliability, the ECD copper in these nanoscale and microscale interconnect features are required to be void-free. Therefore, a technology named “super-conformal” or “bottom-up” copper electroplating has been developed and widely applied in industrial practice. The electroplating process was carried out in an acid copper electrolyte, which was composed of copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, chloride, and trace organic additives. Though the organic additives’ amounts in the electrolytes are very small (generally at several parts per million), the additives play a crucial role in the super-conformal electroplating. The competitive adsorption and differential distribution of the additives on the cathode surface are the origination for the realization of “bottom-up” copper filling electroplating.

text: According to the additives’ different electrochemical effects in the electroplating, the additives were categorized as accelerators, suppressors, and levelers, respectively. Bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [3,4] and its reduced monomer sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [5,6] are most widely used accelerators. In electroplating, the accelerators can reduce the cathodic polarization and facilitate the copper reduction [7,8]. The suppressors are usually polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [9,10], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [11,12], or their copolymers [13,14]. In contrast to the accelerators, the suppressors synergistically work with chloride ions to increase the cathodic polarization and thus suppress the copper reduction. Leveler is another important additive used in the electrolyte to fulfill the super-conformal electroplating, which usually are nitrogencontaining molecules and positively charged in the acid electroplating solution. As reported, the levelers can adsorb at the highdensity charge region of the cathode to inhibit the copper deposition and level the copper surface [15]. In addition, the use of a leveler in the microvia filling electroplating solution can greatly expand the application concentration range of accelerators [16].

text: Currently, most of the reported levelers are nitrogen-containing dyes, such as the Janus Green B (JGB) [17], Alcian Blue (ABPV) [18,19], and Diazine Black (DB)[16] etc., or non-dye heterocyclic aromatic molecules, such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT)[20] and 2-mercaptopyridine (2-MP)[21,22] etc. Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear yet, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. More and more research groups began to purposefully design and synthesize various nitrogen-containing levelers to study their structureproperty relationship [23–27]. In our previous study, we reported a triphenylmethane-based leveler TPM-1, in which three pyrrolidine rings (nitrogen-containing functional groups) were linked by a triphenylmethane (TPM) backbone [28]. It was found that the small molecule with three saturated tertiary amines already be able to show strong inhibition effect and promising microvia filling performance in the copper electroplating experiments.

text: To further investigate the structural influence of nitrogencontaining groups on their electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance, a series of novel TPM-based molecules with different nitrogen-containing functional groups were designed and synthesized. As shown in Fig. 1, TPM-1 and TPM-3 are tertiary amines with pyrrolidine and piperidine as the nitrogen-containing groups, respectively. TPM-2, TPM-4, and TPM-5 are quaternary ammoniums, in which TPM-2 and TPM-5 were methylated base on TPM-1 with I− and Cl− as the counter anions, respectively, and TPM-4 was methylated from TPM-3. In this study, the TPM-based molecules were used as levelers in the super-conformal copper electroplating and their structure-property relationship were carefully investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments.

text: The electrochemical properties of TPM-based levelers were investigated with GMs and CVS methods. Fig. 2 shows the GMs with different injection orders of Cl−, PEG, SPS and TPM-based levelers. As shown in Fig. 2a, with the addition of 40 ppm Cl^-, 200 ppm PEG, and 2 ppm SPS in sequence, the cathode potential went through three changes: rising, sharply decreasing, and slowly rising again. The results are consistent with the literature reports [5,7]: Cl− itself is a depolarizer; however, the Cl− and PEG will synergistically form a barrier layer on the cathode and significantly suppress the copper reduction; SPS is a depolarizer in the presence of Cl−, which can gradually replace the suppressor layer on the cathode leading to a slowly potential increase.

text: Following the addition of SPS, 1.484 μmol/L TPM-based levelers were injected into the electroplating solution. The cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.673 and 0.712 V for TPM-1 and TPM-2, respectively, which imply that at the same concentration, the inhibition effect of the quaternary ammonium TPM-2 was much stronger than the tertiary amine TPM-1. Comparing the molecular structures of TPM-1 and TPM-2, two differences were found: the quaternary ammonium structure and the I− ion. It has been reported that counter anion in a leveler influence its electrochemical behavior and I− can inhibite the Cu ^ 2 + reduction [29– 33]. To distinguish the stronger inhibition ability of TPM-2 was induced by the ammonium structure or I−, we designed and synthesized a new molecule TPM-5, which have the same cationic structure as TPM-2 but with Cl− instead of I− as the counter ion. When TPM-5 was injected in the copper electroplating solution, the potential drops from 0.559 to 0.654 V (fast adsorption) and then slowly moves back to 0.547 V(gradually deactivated by the SPS through the ion pairing interactions)[34–36]. The result indicates that though with the same cationic skeleton, TPM-5 has a much weaker inhibition effect against SPS than TPM-2. As shown in Fig. 2a, the steady potential after addition of TPM-5 is close to the initial value before the leveler injection, which means the adsorption of TPM-5 on the copper surface is weak and the adsorbed leveler was replaced by SPS gradually in the electroplating process. From the GMs of TPM-2 and TPM-5, it can be concluded that the extraordinarily strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 should be related to the anion I− instead of causing by the quaternized pyrrolidine group. In addition, from Fig. 2a, we can see that the inhibition effect of TPM-5 is also weaker than TPM-1. Therefore, by comparing the molecular structures and inhibition abilities of TPM-1, TPM-2 and TPM-5, it was found that the methylated quaternary ammonium structure actually weakens the leveler’s inhibition effect instead of strengthening it, and the exist of I− is the cause of dramatical improvement of the molecule’s inhibition ability.

text: TPM-3, in which three six-membered piperidine rings were introduced to replace the five-membered pyrrolidine rings in TPM-1, has also been added in the electroplating solution to investigate how the ring size of the nitrogen-containing groups affect their electrochemical properties. As shown in Fig. 2a, with the addition of TPM-3, the cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.646 V and then slowly moves back to 0.590 V. The results show that the antagonistic effect of TPM-3 against SPS is weaker than the TPM-1. Since the electronic structures of nitrogen atoms in pyrrolidine and piperidine are very close (the pKa value of pyrrolidine and piperidine are 11.27 and 11.22, respectievely [37]), the electrochemical property difference of TPM-1 and TPM-3 should mainly be caused by the steric hindrance, that is, a bigger head group of the nitrogen-containing group leads to a weaker antagonistic effect against SPS. While for the TPM-4, which also has I− as the counter ion, no surprise, the addition of the molecule leading to a strong polarization and the potential sharply drops to approximately 0.712 V just as TPM-2.

text: To further verify the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the I− alone or the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, equivalent amount of I− as in TPM-2 and TPM-4 was injected into the electroplating solution. As shown in Fig. 2a, the addition of I− alone in the presence of Cl−, PEG, and SPS leads a further polarization from 0.559 to 0.662 V, which means I− has a certain kind of antagonistic against SPS, however, the inhibiton ability is much weaker than that of TPM-2 and TPM-4 as shown in the GMs. The results clearly indicate that the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergistic effect of I− and its counterpart rather than I− itself alone. To further confirm whether the synergistic effect is related the quaternary ammoiunm structure, TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− with a molar ratio of 1:3 have aslo been injected together into the electroplating solution, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2a, with iodide ions in the electrolyte, the potentials of TPM-1 and TPM-3 also dramatically decreased to 0.710 V and 0.713 V, respectively. The polarization of TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− behaved very similarly as TPM-2 and TPM-4. Since TPM-1 and TPM-3 have no quaternary ammonium structure, the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 should be caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the whole structure of the TPM-based counterpart, rather than specifically interacted with the quaternary ammonium structures.

text: GMs with injection orders of Cl−, TPM-based levelers, PEG, and SPS has also been carried out to investigate the synergistic interaction of the TPM-based levelers with Cl− and PEG without the interference of SPS. As shown in Fig. 2b, following the addition of Cl−, the subsequent injection of TPM-based levelers leaded to potential decreases of approximately 93 mV (for TPM-1), 75 mV (for TPM-2, TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, and TPM-3 I−), 100 mV (for TPM-3), 88 mV (for TPM-5), and 49 mV (for I−), respectively. Comparing the inhibition ability of the TPM-1, TPM-2, TPM-5, and I ^ -,, it can be found that in the presence of Cl−, I− leads to the weakest inhibition effect, the TPM-2 (quaternary ammonium salt with I as counter ion) exhibit weaker inhibition effect than TPM-5 (quaternary ammonium salt with Cl− as counter ion), which is further weaker than TPM-1 (tertary amine). Then 200 ppm PEG was added into the electroplating solution. For all TPM-based levelers, the potentials sharply decreased to approximately 0.702 V, which were much lower than the potentials obtained by PEG and Cl− in the absence of TPM-based levelers (approximately 0.667 V, as shown in Fig. 2a). The results imply that the TPM-based levelers synergistically interact with halides and PEG to form stronger barrier layers than those formed by PEG and Cl−. While for the I−,the potential gradually moved back to 0.678 V after the sharp decrease, which is higher than that induced by TPM-based leveler. Finally, SPS was added into the electrolyte and it was found that with TPM-1, TPM-3, TPM-5, and I− presented in the electroplating solution, the cathodic potentials increased by 37 mV, 108 mV, 143 mV, and 39 mV, respectively. While for the electroplating solution contain TPM-2, TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, and TPM-3 I−, instead of increase, the cathodic potential even slightly decreased. These results indicated that with the participate of I−, the TPM-based levelers could synergistically interact with PEG and Cl− forming much stronger barrier layers than those formed by TPM-based levelers without I−. SPS can hardly replace the complex inhibitors composed of PEG, Cl−, and TPM-2 (or TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, TPM-3 I−), which further demonstrated that the combination of iodide ion and TPM-based levelers rather than any of them alone strongly improve the leveler’s inhibition effect and quenched the activity of SPS on the cathodic surface. To make the interactions more comprehensible, a schematic diagram was provided in Fig. 3.

text: To charactrized the effect of the leveler concentrations on its electrochemical properties, cyclic voltammetry measurements with various concentrations of TPM-based levelers (or I−) in an electroplating solution containing 2 ppm SPS, 40 ppm Cl− and 200 ppm PEG have been carried out. As shown in Fig. 4, the increase of the TPM-based levelers (or I−) concentration all leads to a further polarization. For TPM-1, the addition of 0.05 ppm leveler not only decreases the absolute current density, but also changes the relative current density values in the forward (negative-going) and backward (positive-going) sweep. As reported, the current densities in the return sweep larger than the forward values indicate a positive feedback for the copper electroplating [38,39]. In addition, when the concentration of TPM-1 reaches as high as 8 ppm, an evident negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon was observed, which has been widely used to explain the mechanism of extremely bottom-up filling of Cu or other metals with one suppressor as the additive in electroplating [38,40–42]. Similarly, NDR has also been observed with other TPM-based levelers at relatively high concentrations (above 2 ppm for TPM-2 and TPM-4; above 8 for TPM-3; above 20 ppm for TPM-5). Though ternary additives (leveler, suppressor, and accelerator) were used in this research instead of one additive system reported in literature, extremely bottom-up microvia filling effect has also been otained with high concentrations of TPM-2 or TPM-4 (as shown in Figs. 7–2f, 7–2g, 7–4f, and 7–4g), which imply a gradual breakdown of the suppression starting from the microvia bottom. NDR is observed for all high concentration TPM-based levelers, however, only TPM-2 and TPM-4 result in the extremely bottom-up filling. One possible explanation is that due to the strong inhibition strength caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, the suppression layer formed by high concentration of TPM-2 (or TPM-4) plays a predominant effect on the cathod surface and overshadowed the effect of SPS (as shown in Fig. 3e and f). While for other TPM-based levelers (or I−), the antagonistic effect of SPS and the inhibitors contributes together to achieve the super-conformal electroplaitng, as described by the curvature enhanced adsorbate coverage (CEAC) [36] or convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) [43] mechanisms.

text: The TPM-based levelers are quaternary ammoniums (TPM-2, TPM-4, and TPM-5) or tertiary amines (TPM-1 and TPM-3), which will all be positively charged and show a certain kind of surface activity in the acid electroplating solution. To better understand adsorption of the TPM-based levelers on the copper surface, contact angle measurements were detected. As shown in Fig. 6, the contact angle of the basic electroplating solution (0.88 mol/L CuSO _4·5H_20 and 0.54 mol/L H_2S0_ 4) on copper surface is 4 5.6 ^ ° With the addition of 1.484 μ mol / L TPM-based levelers, the contact angles of the electroplating solution all decreased and the values for TPM-1, TPM-2, TPM-3, TPM-4, TPM-5 are 2 7.4 ^ °, 2 3.8 ^ °, 3 2.9 ^ °, 2 3.5 ^ °, 3 6.2 ~ ~ \textdegree ~,, respectively. Generally, a smaller contact angle of an electroplating solution indicates a stronger surface activity of the TPMbased leveler, and denser adsorbed leveler layers were formed on the copper interface, which will lead to a stronger inhibition effect of the leveler. As shown in Fig. 6, the contact angle values followed in an order: leveler free > TPM-5 > TPM-3 > TPM-1 > TPM-2 TPM-4, which are in good accordance with the electrochemical measurement results.

text: As reported, the electromigration resistance of copper film is affected largely by the (111) orientation [45,46]. The crystalline structure of the copper depositions electroplated with various TPMbased levelers were characterized by XRD. As shown in Fig. 9, without leveler in the electroplating solution, the preferred crystalline orientation of the copper layer is Cu (111). When TPM-1 was added in the electroplating solution, the predominant texture peak was changed from Cu (111) to Cu (220), which means the leveler TPM-1 can hinder the growth of Cu (111). Different from TPM-1, the preferred crystalline orientation of the copper layers deposited with TPM-2, TPM-3, TPM-4 and TPM-5 as levelers is Cu (111) again. Considering the molecular structures, electrochemical properties, and the crystalline orientations, the nitrogen-containing groups in a leveler not only affect its adsorption strength on the copper surface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different crystalline plane.

text: 4. Conclusions

text: In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− Cl^- as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.
